items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Let’s say Miss Donegan. There was one.

ctx.x: I hope so. [laughs] What about some of the ones would you consider, when I said difficult, I don’t mean everybody was just fighting you every way, it’s just something that made it a little more, where you had to be a little more spontaneous, reinvent yourself right on the air or something like that.

Oh man. Let’s say Miss Donegan. There was one. She . . . that woman. She did a great show, but she was so eager to outplay me that in the middle of the show I started to get a headache. I took a break and went to the ladies’ room. Took an aspirin and said, “Come on now. Shape up.” At one point I played a tune, and she said, “I really like

that tune. I’d like to play you my version of it.” I said, “Fine, o.k., go ahead.” So at the end of the show, I said to her, “Dorothy, don’t worry, you win.” She says . . . now I can’t think of the tag line. She said, “No contest,” in a very haughty way.

items.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Marian McPartland, people like that you know.

ctx.x: Who were some of the other women on that performance, do you recall?
Marian McPartland, people like that you know.
It’s still pretty rare to see more than one woman jazz musician on stage at any time. Do you think that having an evening of performances by women artists, is that a good thing or not necessarily?
